Rapper and chef Action Bronson joins Joe Rogan for episode 2487. Bronson pairs heavy rhymes with a deep love of food. His shows mix eating, travel, and pure joy.

Rogan, a keen eater and hunter, meets him on rich ground. They trade tales of meals, kitchens, and wild appetites. Bronson tells how Queens and fine food shaped one man. The episode is flavorful in every sense. Food fans and hip-hop heads alike get a guest who lives both lives at full volume, with gusto. Few guests love food with his open joy.
uslaw-usc-t2-s143a:
Section 143a of Title 2 lists ways Library of Congress funds may be disbursed, effective from October 1, 1978. One use reimburses the Department of State for medical services given to Library employees stationed abroad. The section sits in Chapter 5 of Title 2, the chapter on the Library of Congress.

Funds may also support contracting for and hiring alien employees for the Library. Their compensation plans must be comparable to plans authorized for Foreign Service hiring. Purchase or hire of passenger motor vehicles is another listed use. Travel, storage, and transport of household goods also qualify. Families en route get transport and per diem support, capped at twenty-four.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1823a:
Section 1823a of Title 2 of the United States Code, in the chapter on the Architect of the Capitol, allows real property to be acquired by lease for the Library of Congress. If funds are available, the Architect may lease property in any State or in the District of Columbia for the Library's use. Two steps must come first.

The Architect and the Librarian must send a joint request for the lease to three bodies. The Joint Committee on the Library must approve it, and so must the Appropriations Committees of both Houses. A second part lets the Architect and the Librarian transfer funds between themselves, with the same approvals, to pay the costs of acquiring property under the section.
uslaw-usc-t2-s183a:
Section 183a of Title 2 of the United States Code provides for an oral history of the House of Representatives to be kept at the Library of Congress. It sits in the chapter on the Library of Congress.

The Librarian of Congress must accept the oral history for deposit. The Librarian must also preserve it, maintain it, and make it open to users. The history tells the story of the House through its members and former members. It is gathered and updated by the United States Association of Former Members of Congress or another private group. That work is done on a voluntary or contract basis, and the Librarian may use the group's help or hire it. The section defines an oral history as personal recollection recorded through interviews, transcripts, or audio and video recordings.
